https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: How the Elon Musk of fish farming hopes to save our smoked salmon
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
When not obscured by sheets of rain, the scenery of Hardangerfjord is spectacular. One of Norway’s most famous fjords, it attracts thousands of tourists a year.
But this picturesque setting will never be seen by the hundreds of thousands of salmon that live beneath the black platform seen below. It’s the tip of the iceberg, the top of a 72-metre tall salmon container whose proponents believe could be the answer to many of the farmed fish’s environmental headaches.
Since the early 1970s, Norway has grown to become the world’s biggest producer of salmon. Around half the salmon the world eats comes from fish raised in open net pens in the cool waters of fjords like Hardangerfjord.
But critics have been warning for decades that it comes with an enormous environmental impact. Tens of millions of farmed fish suffer and die annually from sea lice, while escapees spread the lice, breed with wild fish and compromise their genetic fitness. Nutrient pollution from fish faeces wreaks havoc on coastal ecology, and treatments used on nets lead to copper and other materials contaminating local waters.
“It’s time for a change, for sure,” said Sondre Eide, CEO of Eide Fjordbruk, which has been fish farming here for more than half a century. The 35-year-old technophile is busy, in his words, “disrupting” his own company by changing how it produces salmon.
Some say change cannot come soon enough. The closure in June of 33 rivers by authorities owing to low salmon counts should serve as an “alarm bell” of the threat if the industry does not change, said Professor Jon Olaf Olaussen from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology.
Vegard Heggem, a former Liverpool FC right-back who owned a Norwegian salmon lodge until two years ago, said the closures were of great concern for wild salmon tourist businesses, which attract visitors from the US to Japan. “I realised the salmon could actually disappear unless we do something. I felt it almost as a physical thing, a horrible sinking realisation,” he said.
Farmed and wild salmon have different genetic markers. Scientists use those to map the degree of genetic introgression — the inroads the genetic material of farmed fish have made into wild ones — at 250 population centres of wild salmon. Only 82 have no traces of farmed salmon. “It’s widespread,” said Sten Ola Karlsson at the Norwegian Institute for Nature Research.
Interbreeding leads to offspring less suited for the wild, with studies finding they have low survival rates in freshwater rivers. Longer term, they could be less likely to cope with the warming waters climate change brings. In Hardangerfjord the problem is so acute some of its wild salmon are kept in an artificial environment, a “living genebank”, or back-up.
These pressures, and a 23 per cent drop in Atlantic salmon numbers between 2006 and 2020, last year saw the species elevated up the global Red List of endangered species. It is now one step closer to extinction.
Eide thinks the answer is simple. End open net salmon farms and switch to ones with closed containers. Across choppy waters, he takes me by boat to one of his conventional open net farms, which sits near a metallic floating visitor centre and restaurant that looks like a Bond villain lair and, fittingly, is called Salmon Eye.
Holding a salmon plucked from the pen with a net, Eide points out a single louse. Salmon mortality from lice, which caused a record number of deaths on Scottish fish farms last year, is relatively low on Eide’s farms. Just 8 per cent die versus 16.7 per cent across the industry, meaning more than 60 million fish dying last year of disease, lice and the treatments designed to tackle them.
Our next stop, about ten minutes away, is a new type of fish farm. Inside, the banks of screens showing swirls of swimming salmon and data look the same as the conventional farm.
But outside, there is the Watermoon, a 30-metre diameter submerged container that would be western Norway’s tallest building if placed on land. The name “sounded good” and is meant to represent a Kennedy-style “moonshot” to transform the salmon industry, Eide said.
The 200,000 fish inside are sealed off from the risk of lice and, in theory, cannot escape. The system collects the solid particles of waste from the fish, reducing the amount of local water pollution — though it cannot yet trap the soluble pollution too. Eide, who namechecks Tesla, SpaceX and the tech industry more than his fellow fish farmers, has spent hundreds of millions of pounds on developing and then building the device.
So far, the mortality rate for fish in the tank is much lower than typical, at under 2 per cent. Raised in the tank since May, the salmon should be harvested in the new year.
Success or failure for the scheme matters for more than just Eide. Farmed salmon contributes about 2 cent to Norwegian GDP by some estimates. Some see it as a way Norway can continue to enjoy one of the best social welfare systems in the world, as the oil and gas industry winds down in coming decades. How Norway’s fish farms fix their problems could also influence big salmon producers in Chile, Canada and Scotland.
Yet travelling back to the docks at Osøyro across stomach-churning waters, even Eide admits he faces myriad hurdles. Chief is cost. The container is about 30 times more expensive than a net. “It’s not economically sustainable to do it. Today it’s economically beneficial to have lice and high deaths,” he said.
Then there is scale. While 200,000 fish may sound like a lot, the tank can theoretically take 300,000 fish and Eide hopes to have a million fish in containers next year. But Norway sold 1.6 million tonnes of salmon last year, equivalent to hundreds of millions of fish.
A fast switch to tanks could hinge on a government proposal on salmon licences, expected in December. Eide wants every open net licence to count as three for closed tanks, as a financial incentive. Not everyone agrees with public support. Rune Jensen, a campaigner who runs the group Salmon Camera, said: “They are well off and could pay for it themselves. As a citizen, why should I co-finance it?”
Containers also do not solve the problem of the millions of tonnes of fish, soya and other material fed to salmon, which Jensen said is unsustainable. Eide is aware of this and some companies are exploring using fly larvae, but he said: “One problem at a time.”
Observers think one of the biggest barriers will be inertia in the wider industry, for fear of eating into profits. Farmed salmon is hugely profitable. The industry had an average profit of 24 per cent from 2018 to 2022, according to market intelligence firm Kontali. Olaf Olaussen calls it a “superprofit”.
Alf-Helge Aarskog, who until 2019 was CEO of the world’s biggest farmed salmon firm, Mowi, said vested interests may slow change. He singles out “wellboats”, the vessels used to treat and rid salmon of lice, which would be obsolete in a closed container world. “We have created a parasite on the parasite,” said Aarskog, who now works for Eide.
While Eide sees Norwegian salmon as the way to provide protein to a growing global population of 9 billion, others said the only sustainable option is to curb the sector.
“The uncomfortable truth is that the total volume has to be reduced substantially if you’re going to take the environmental issues seriously. That’s a tall order with this government, or the previous, because they make too much money,” said Pål Fidjestol from the Norwegian Society for the Conservation of Nature, the country’s oldest environmental group.
Per Espen Stoknes, a former Green Party MP and associate professor at the Norwegian Business School, said the industry is on a “suicidal track” if it continues with minor tinkering, and a bold move to closed systems is needed. “I think the industry has a very bright future, but it is not investing anywhere near enough in the solutions.”
The Norwegian ministry of fisheries and the country’s biggest industry body, the Norwegian Seafood Federation, were contacted for comment.
Beyond fish and oil and gas, Norway is famous for its incredibly fast transition from polluting cars to electric ones. The fact that more than 90 per cent of new cars are now electric is because of early incentives, from tax breaks to free parking and being allowed to drive in bus lanes. Eide believes the switchover to a cleaner way of producing salmon will only happen quickly with a similar economic support.
“Nobody in Norway bought an electric car only because of the environmental factor. This doesn’t happen by itself,” he said.
